views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold Lists 1–3 where they sit and do not fire the threatened ~$267B phase-three package. Reopen a Liu He / Lighthizer channel aimed at a possible late-November Trump–Xi meeting, but make any pause in the January 1 lift of List 3 from 10% to 25% contingent on verifiable movement on forced tech transfer and IP—not another purchase MOU. Spending the remaining consumer-goods ammunition now would hit U.S. households into the holidays and midterms while giving Beijing an easy nationalist rally, and rolling anything back before talks would throw away the only leverage that has actually been built.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is slightly opportunity-leaning, not high. The Section 301 record (22 Mar) still documents a real long-run IP/tech-transfer problem, and China has now matched through ~$60B of U.S. goods at 5–10% (24 Sep) after earlier 25% hits on soybeans, autos, and aircraft. That farm exposure is the main U.S. vulnerability: China takes ~60% of U.S. soybean exports (~$14B), prices have fallen toward break-even, and farm-state Republicans are restless. But the U.S. macro is not breaking—Michigan sentiment is 100.1, industrial production is up, VIX is 12.89—while China is showing more strain (yuan ~6.88, +9.5% vs April; IP slowing to 105.8; reserves down ~1.2%). U.S. goods exports to China are already off ~7%, but imports from China have surged ~31% on front-running, so the bilateral deficit is wider, not narrower. Asymmetry still favors Washington: combined 301 coverage is ~$250B of Chinese imports versus China’s remaining U.S. import base of roughly $130B, and the unused January 25% clock plus a held $267B threat is more useful as a bargaining chip than as an immediate levy on phones, toys, and holiday goods. The May 19 joint statement showed Beijing will offer purchases and then walk; the 29 May collapse showed purchases-without-structure is not a settlement. Action therefore stays at zero: talk without new U.S. commitments, keep the January hike as the next pressure point, and do not concede or escalate further until China puts structural offers on the table.
key_factors: List 3 ($200B at 10%) just took effect 24 Sep; combined 301 coverage ~$250B; Jan 1 hike to 25% is unused leverage
China retaliated on ~$60B at 5–10% and has largely exhausted dollar-for-dollar matching capacity
U.S. economy still firm (sentiment 100.1, IP rising, VIX ~13); China showing FX, IP, and reserve strain
Soybean/farm-belt retaliation is the binding U.S. political and export cost; farmers want markets not aid
May 19 purchase-truce collapsed within 10 days; structural IP/tech-transfer demands remain unmet
Phase-three (~$267B) would hit consumer electronics into holidays/midterms; industry warned it lands on the U.S.
Possible Trump–Xi meeting at G20 late November is the natural talk window

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory.
U.S. consumer sentiment 100.1 (Sep 2018), up from 96.2 in August — no demand shock visible yet.
U.S. goods exports to China down to $9.73B (Sep) from $10.51B (Apr), -7.4% over the window.
U.S. goods imports from China up to $49.94B (Sep) from $38.23B (Apr), +30.6% — front-running of List 3.
CNY/USD 6.8763 on 26 Sep vs 6.2785 on 2 Apr, +9.5% — yuan move largely offsets a 10% List 3 tariff.
China industrial production index slowed from 107.0 (Apr) to 105.8 (Sep).
If China takes retaliatory action against our farmers or other industries, we will immediately pursue phase three, which is tariffs on approximately $267 billion of additional imports.
Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in late November at the G-20; Mnuchin invited Liu He for talks; China said it would retaliate on ~$60B including LNG.
Soybean prices fell from ~$11/bu earlier in the year to under $9; China essentially halted new purchases; farmers dismissed $12B aid and want trade restored.
